ENGINEERING.whatItMeasures: Interest in engineering describes attraction to designing, building and improving things that work. It covers curiosity about how machines and systems function, satisfaction in solving a practical problem, and willingness to work through the mathematics and physics that underpin a design. This indicates interest, not aptitude or eligibility for any course.
looksLike: Wants to know how a machine or system works
Enjoys building, assembling or fixing
Interested in improving how something is done
Comfortable with mathematics applied to real problems
Notices design flaws in everyday objects
ENGINEERING.learningImplications: Engineering interest is best supported by keeping mathematics and physics strong while doing something practical alongside them. Projects where theory produces a working result convert abstract study into motivation. Robotics, electronics and design software give a realistic taste of the work well before a course has to be chosen.
activities: Join a robotics or electronics club
Build a small project end to end and document it
Learn CAD or simulation software basics
Take apart and reassemble a working device
Talk to a practising engineer about a normal working day
ENGINEERING.parentTip: Support the practical side rather than only the entrance-exam side. A student who builds things stays motivated through the years of mathematics and physics that engineering requires. Conversations with working engineers give a far more realistic picture of the field than coaching-class marketing does.
ENGINEERING.studentTip: Build something small, completely, and write up how it works. That teaches more about whether you want this field than any amount of reading. Keep mathematics and physics strong, because they are the gate. Try several branches before deciding, since mechanical, electrical and software work feel very different day to day.

TECHNOLOGY.whatItMeasures: Interest in technology describes attraction to computing, software, data and digital systems. It covers curiosity about how applications and networks work, enjoyment of building or automating something, and comfort learning new tools independently. It reflects what a student is drawn to rather than what they are currently able to do.
looksLike: Curious about how software or the internet works
Tries new applications and tools independently
Enjoys automating or simplifying a repetitive task
Comfortable teaching themselves from online resources
Interested in data, systems or security
TECHNOLOGY.learningImplications: Technology interest rewards self-directed practice more than most fields, because tools and resources are freely available. Building small working projects teaches faster than passive tutorials. Mathematics and logical reasoning support it, and writing matters more than students expect, since technical work has to be explained to non-technical people.
development: Finishing projects rather than starting many
Explaining technical work to non-technical people
Building depth in fundamentals, not only tools
Working within a team codebase or standard
activities: Learn one programming language properly through projects
Build and finish a small application or website
Take part in a hackathon or coding competition
Contribute to or read an open-source project
Explain a technical concept to someone non-technical
TECHNOLOGY.parentTip: Distinguish between consuming technology and building with it; the second is what indicates genuine interest. Screen time spent building a project is not the same as screen time spent scrolling. Encourage finishing one project rather than starting many, since a completed piece of work is what demonstrates ability later.
TECHNOLOGY.studentTip: Build things and finish them. One completed project teaches more than ten tutorials and, unlike marks, it is something you can show. Learn the fundamentals rather than only the currently fashionable tool. Practise explaining what you built to someone non-technical, because that skill separates good engineers from unemployed ones.

MEDICAL.whatItMeasures: Interest in medical and healthcare work describes attraction to understanding the human body, diagnosing problems and caring for people who are unwell. It combines scientific curiosity with a wish to help directly. It indicates interest only, and says nothing about eligibility, aptitude for entrance examinations, or suitability for clinical practice.
looksLike: Curious about how the body works and why illness happens
Comfortable around people who are unwell
Interested in biology beyond the syllabus
Wants work with a visible human benefit
Careful and methodical with detail
MEDICAL.learningImplications: Medical interest needs biology and chemistry kept strong, alongside genuine exposure to healthcare settings. The reality of the work, long training, shift patterns, emotional demands, is worth understanding early. Volunteering or shadowing gives a far more accurate picture than television or family expectation does.
development: Building resilience for emotionally demanding work
Exploring the full range of health careers, not only medicine
activities: Volunteer or shadow in a healthcare setting if permitted
Read about the daily reality of clinical work
Keep biology and chemistry strong
Learn basic first aid properly
Talk to people in several health professions, not only doctors
MEDICAL.parentTip: Help this student see the whole field rather than one prestigious role. Nursing, physiotherapy, pharmacy, biomedical research and public health are substantial careers with different entry routes and working lives. Real exposure to a healthcare setting is worth more than years of assumption, in either direction.
MEDICAL.studentTip: Get real exposure before committing, since healthcare work is very different from how it looks from outside. Keep biology and chemistry strong. Look at the whole field rather than one job title, because several health professions may suit you better and have different entry routes. Understand the training length before you choose.

PSYCHOLOGY.whatItMeasures: Interest in psychology describes attraction to understanding why people think, feel and behave as they do. It covers curiosity about motivation and behaviour, interest in listening to people's experiences, and willingness to study behaviour systematically rather than relying on intuition. It is an interest indicator only.
looksLike: Curious about why people behave as they do
People confide in them
Interested in behaviour, motivation and emotion
Notices patterns in how people react
Wants to understand rather than judge
PSYCHOLOGY.learningImplications: Psychology is a science, and students are often surprised by how much statistics and research method it involves. Keeping mathematics reasonable matters. Reading actual psychological research rather than popular articles gives a realistic picture. Listening skills can be practised long before any formal training begins.
development: Comfort with statistics and research method
activities: Read introductory psychology from a reputable source
Practise listening without offering advice
Keep mathematics and statistics reasonable
Volunteer in a peer-support or helpline-style role if available
Talk to a practising psychologist or counsellor
PSYCHOLOGY.parentTip: Take this interest seriously; psychology is a rigorous scientific field with wide application, not a soft option. Point out the statistics and research involved so the choice is informed. Practising real listening at home, hearing them out fully before responding, both supports the interest and models the skill.
PSYCHOLOGY.studentTip: Psychology involves more statistics and research method than most people expect, so keep your mathematics reasonable. Read actual research rather than popular psychology articles. Practise listening without jumping to advice, it is harder than it sounds and it is the core skill. Understand the qualification route early, since it is long.

TEACHING.whatItMeasures: Interest in teaching describes attraction to helping others learn: explaining clearly, noticing where someone is stuck, and finding satisfaction when understanding arrives. It covers patience with the process of learning and interest in a subject deep enough to want to pass it on.
looksLike: Enjoys explaining things to classmates
Patient when someone does not understand
Notices where a person is actually stuck
Finds different ways to explain the same idea
Satisfied when someone else succeeds
TEACHING.learningImplications: Teaching interest is directly useful while still a student, because explaining material is one of the most effective ways to learn it. Peer tutoring builds both the subject knowledge and the skill. Depth in at least one subject matters, since teaching well requires knowing considerably more than is being taught.
development: Managing a group, not only individuals
Handling varied ability in one room
Understanding the realities of the profession
activities: Tutor a younger student regularly
Explain a topic three different ways
Take a subject deeper than the syllabus requires
Lead a study group session
Talk to teachers about the profession honestly
TEACHING.parentTip: Peer tutoring is genuine practice and genuine revision at the same time, so encourage it rather than seeing it as time taken from their own study. Encourage depth in one subject, since teaching requires knowing well beyond what is taught. Honest conversations with working teachers give a realistic view of the profession.
TEACHING.studentTip: Teaching someone else is the fastest way to find out what you do not know, so use it as a study method now. Go deeper in at least one subject than the syllabus requires. Practise explaining the same idea in several different ways, since the second explanation is usually the one that works.

MANAGEMENT.whatItMeasures: Interest in management describes attraction to organising people, resources and processes towards a result. It covers planning, coordinating, making decisions and taking responsibility for how a group performs. It reflects the kind of work someone is drawn to, not their current capability as a leader.
looksLike: Organises people and tasks naturally
Comfortable being responsible for a result
Thinks about how to make a process work better
Enjoys planning and coordinating
Steps in when a group lacks direction
MANAGEMENT.learningImplications: Management interest is best developed through real responsibility rather than theory. Running an event, leading a project, or managing a club budget teaches more than reading about leadership. Numeracy and communication both matter, and experiencing the consequences of a plan that did not work is a large part of the learning.
activities: Lead a school event or club end to end
Manage a real budget for an activity
Take a coordinating role in a group project
Review after a project what you would change
Learn spreadsheet and planning basics
MANAGEMENT.parentTip: Give real responsibility with real consequences, since management is learned by doing rather than by being told. Let them run something and let it go imperfectly. Ask what they would do differently next time, because the review is where most of the learning happens rather than in the event itself.
MANAGEMENT.studentTip: Run something real, a club, an event, a project, and see it through to the end including the parts that are dull. Learn to delegate rather than doing everything yourself; it feels slower and it is the actual skill. Review honestly afterwards, because that is where you improve.

ENTREPRENEURSHIP.whatItMeasures: Interest in entrepreneurship describes attraction to starting and building something of your own. It covers spotting an unmet need, willingness to act without guarantees, comfort with uncertainty, and persistence through early failure. It is an interest indicator and not a prediction of commercial success.
looksLike: Notices problems and thinks about solving them commercially
Starts small ventures or projects
Comfortable with uncertainty and risk
Persistent after something does not work
Prefers building own thing to following instructions
ENTREPRENEURSHIP.learningImplications: Entrepreneurial interest is best served by small real attempts rather than by theory. Selling something, running an event, or building a small service teaches customer, cost and delivery realities quickly. Basic financial literacy and communication both matter more than any business vocabulary learned in advance.
development: Following through past the exciting stage
Listening to customers rather than assuming
Building a team rather than working alone
activities: Run one small venture end to end and count the money honestly
Interview ten potential users before building anything
Learn basic accounting and pricing
Enter a business plan or startup competition
Talk to someone who runs a small business
ENTREPRENEURSHIP.parentTip: Let small ventures happen and let them fail cheaply, since that is the least expensive education available in this area. Insist on honest accounting, including their own time, because a venture that looks profitable often is not. Follow-through past the exciting first weeks is the habit most worth encouraging.
ENTREPRENEURSHIP.studentTip: Start something small and real rather than planning something large and hypothetical. Talk to potential customers before you build. Count your costs honestly, including your own time. Expect the first attempt to fail and treat it as tuition. The rare skill is not having ideas, it is finishing them.

COMMERCE.whatItMeasures: Interest in commerce describes attraction to business, trade, money and how organisations operate financially. It covers curiosity about pricing, profit, markets and financial records, and comfort working with numbers in a business context rather than a purely mathematical one.
looksLike: Interested in how businesses make money
Comfortable with numbers applied to money
Notices pricing, offers and market behaviour
Enjoys keeping accounts or records accurately
Follows business or financial news
COMMERCE.learningImplications: Commerce interest is supported by accuracy, numeracy and organisation. Accounting rewards systematic work more than brilliance. Practical exposure, handling a real budget, tracking a small portfolio on paper, or keeping accounts for a club, makes abstract concepts concrete and shows quickly whether the daily work appeals.
development: Interpreting numbers, not only recording them
Keeping up with regulation and change
activities: Keep accounts for a club or family project
Track a hypothetical investment portfolio on paper
Learn spreadsheet skills properly
Follow business news weekly and summarise one story
Talk to an accountant or banker about daily work
COMMERCE.parentTip: Give this student real financial responsibility at a manageable scale: a budget to manage, accounts to keep, a purchase to research and justify. Commerce careers reward accuracy and consistency, so habits of careful record keeping built now matter more than early technical vocabulary.
COMMERCE.studentTip: Get practical: keep real accounts for something, track a portfolio on paper, manage an actual budget. Learn spreadsheets properly, they are the working tool of the whole field. Practise explaining what numbers mean rather than only producing them, since interpretation is what gets valued as you progress.

ARTS.whatItMeasures: Interest in the arts describes attraction to creative and cultural work: making, performing, interpreting and understanding artistic expression. It covers enjoyment of producing original work and interest in the traditions and craft behind an art form. It indicates interest rather than measured artistic ability.
looksLike: Makes things without being asked to
Interested in culture, style and artistic traditions
Prefers open-ended creative tasks
Notices craft and technique in others' work
Expresses ideas through a chosen medium
ARTS.learningImplications: Arts interest is best supported by regular practice and by building a body of finished work. The technical craft underneath the creativity matters and is often underestimated. Studying the history and context of an art form deepens the work. A portfolio of completed pieces is usually what opens doors, more than marks.
development: Understanding the professional side of creative work
activities: Keep an ongoing portfolio of finished pieces
Study the technical craft behind your art form
Enter exhibitions or competitions
Seek critique and revise one piece properly
Learn about how creative work is actually commissioned and paid
ARTS.parentTip: Treat this as a field with real careers and real training rather than as a hobby to be set aside at exam time. Support the craft, classes, materials, exposure to good work, and encourage finished pieces. A portfolio of completed work is the currency of creative fields, more than any single mark.
ARTS.studentTip: Finish things. A portfolio of completed pieces is what gets you taken seriously, and unfinished ideas count for nothing. Build the technical craft under the creativity, since inspiration without skill stalls. Learn how creative work actually gets commissioned and paid, because that knowledge is what makes it a career.

DESIGN.whatItMeasures: Interest in design describes attraction to shaping how things look and work for the people who use them. It covers noticing what is well or badly designed, caring about both appearance and usability, and enjoying the process of iterating towards something better. It sits between creative and practical work.
looksLike: Notices when something is badly designed
Cares about how things work, not only how they look
Redesigns or improves existing things
Interested in what users find confusing
Iterates rather than settling for the first version
DESIGN.learningImplications: Design interest is developed through making and revising. Producing several versions of the same piece teaches more than starting many new ones. Understanding the user matters as much as visual skill, so getting real feedback on work is central. A portfolio showing process, not only outcomes, is what design courses and employers look for.
development: Testing with real users rather than assuming
Working within a brief and constraints
Documenting the process, not only the result
activities: Redesign something you find frustrating and explain why
Learn a design tool properly
Show work to real users and revise from feedback
Keep a portfolio showing process and iterations
Study why a well-known design works
DESIGN.parentTip: Design is a substantial professional field with strong demand, particularly in digital product work. Support tools and exposure to good design. Encourage testing work on real people, since design is judged by whether it works for a user rather than by whether the designer likes it.
DESIGN.studentTip: Design is judged by whether it works for someone else, so put your work in front of real people and revise from what they struggle with. Keep a portfolio that shows your process and iterations, not only polished final images; courses and employers want to see how you think.

GOVERNMENT.whatItMeasures: Interest in government and public service describes attraction to how societies are organised and governed, and to work that serves the public. It covers curiosity about policy, law and administration, and motivation to contribute at a community or national scale rather than only individually.
looksLike: Follows news, policy and current affairs
Interested in fairness, rights and how rules are made
Wants to contribute at community or national level
Comfortable with formal processes and institutions
Argues about how things ought to be organised
GOVERNMENT.learningImplications: This interest is supported by strong reading, writing and general awareness. History, civics, economics and language all contribute. Competitive public-service examinations reward broad, sustained reading over years rather than late preparation, so a habit of following current affairs seriously is genuinely useful early.
development: Understanding multiple sides of a policy issue
activities: Follow serious news daily and summarise one issue weekly
Join debate or a model United Nations activity
Read about how a law or policy is actually made
Take part in student government
Talk to someone working in public administration
GOVERNMENT.parentTip: Encourage broad, serious reading and real discussion of current affairs, since these careers reward general awareness accumulated over years. Discuss issues from more than one side rather than only your own view. Be realistic together about the length and competitiveness of public-service examination routes.
GOVERNMENT.studentTip: Read widely and seriously, starting now; these routes reward years of accumulated awareness rather than last-minute preparation. Practise arguing a position you disagree with, because understanding both sides is the actual skill. Get involved in student government to see how slow institutional processes really feel.

HOSPITALITY.whatItMeasures: Interest in hospitality describes attraction to travel, service, events and looking after people's experience. It covers enjoyment of making an occasion work, comfort with people from varied backgrounds, and satisfaction in service delivered well. It is an interest indicator rather than an assessment of suitability.
looksLike: Enjoys hosting, organising or looking after guests
Comfortable with people from varied backgrounds
Notices details that make an experience better
Interested in travel, food or events
Stays composed when something goes wrong
HOSPITALITY.learningImplications: Hospitality interest benefits from languages, communication and practical experience. Helping run real events shows quickly whether the long hours and constant people contact appeal. The field rewards composure under pressure and attention to detail, both of which can be practised well before any formal training.
strengths: Service orientation and attention to detail
activities: Help organise a real event start to finish
Learn an additional language
Work or volunteer in a service role if permitted
Study how a hotel or restaurant actually operates
Practise staying composed when a plan fails
HOSPITALITY.parentTip: Hospitality is an international industry with structured management careers, not only front-line service work. Let them help run real events, which tests interest quickly. Be realistic together about hours and shift patterns, since that is what most often surprises people entering the field.
HOSPITALITY.studentTip: Help run a real event from start to finish; that will tell you within a weekend whether this suits you. Learn another language, it opens the international side of the field. Practise composure when things go wrong, because in this work something always does and that moment is the job.

ENVIRONMENT.whatItMeasures: Interest in the environment describes attraction to the natural world, sustainability and the systems that connect them. It covers concern about environmental issues, curiosity about ecosystems and climate, and motivation to work on problems at that scale. It indicates interest rather than scientific aptitude.
looksLike: Concerned about environmental and climate issues
Curious about ecosystems and how they interact
Prefers outdoor and field-based activity
Notices waste and inefficiency
Wants work with a visible environmental purpose
ENVIRONMENT.learningImplications: Environmental interest is supported by biology, chemistry, geography and increasingly by data skills, since much environmental work is measurement and analysis. Fieldwork and citizen-science projects give realistic exposure. Understanding that the field spans science, policy, engineering and law helps a student find the entry route that suits them.
development: Building the data and analysis skills the field requires
activities: Join a citizen-science or conservation project
Run a waste or energy audit at school or home
Keep field observation records properly
Learn basic data analysis
Explore the policy and legal side, not only the science
ENVIRONMENT.parentTip: Support real involvement rather than only concern: a conservation project, a garden, a measured audit of household energy. Point out that this field includes engineering, law, data and policy as well as field science, which widens the realistic routes in considerably.
ENVIRONMENT.studentTip: Get involved in something measurable rather than only caring about the issue. Learn data skills, since much environmental work is measurement and analysis. Explore the policy, law and engineering sides too, as they often have more direct routes in and more influence than field science alone.
